title: The #1 Problem with New Years Life-Changey Stuff - Clarity of Purpose
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that resolutions, one-word themes and goals all fail without clarity of purpose, and that the same deficiency wrecks school improvement initiatives and literacy frameworks. He borrows the evidence from Greg McKeown's Essentialism, which reports that clarity of purpose consistently predicts how people do their jobs and that without it people waste energy on the trivial many. He then supplies his own case, tracing his purpose from the vague ambition of making a positive impact on students' lives in 2006 to the sharper formulation of promoting long-term student flourishing. The practical payoff is a filter, and he shows it operating on three teacher decisions: lesson planning becomes five things all year long rather than hitting every standard, task triage asks which required work actually promotes long-term flourishing and which merely keeps the job, and late-night grading loses to sleep and family on the grounds that modelling a balanced life is itself a way of promoting flourishing. The closing contrast is the argument's proof: he cannot recall his 2015 goals without checking a spreadsheet, but he can state his purpose instantly and identically every time. He also reports seeing educators languishing for lack of clear purpose and students frustrated by what they see as the purposelessness of high school. The advice is to start with purpose and let goals follow.
points: Stuart's triage question is the reusable artefact: which required tasks are most likely to promote long-term student flourishing, with everything non-negotiable but unimportant completed under heavy time minimisation.
He treats purpose as a substitute for standards-coverage planning, replacing a hit-every-standard approach with a small set of things practised all year long.

The test he applies to himself is memory, since goals needed a spreadsheet to recall while purpose could be stated identically a hundred times, which he offers as the practical marker of real clarity.
He extends the diagnosis past individuals to institutions, naming school improvement initiatives and literacy frameworks as the places where absent purpose does the most damage.
Choosing sleep and family over midnight grading is defended not as self-care but as modelling a flourishing life for students, which folds teacher workload into the purpose itself.
quotes: Maybe you're a “ one word ” person, or a classic resolution-setter, or a jaded New Years apathist. Regardless, here's all I have to say: without clarity of purpose, resolutions, goals and words are destined to disappoint. Importantly, this principle extends way beyond efforts at personal improvement; clarity of purpose is critical with things like school improvement initiatives and literacy frameworks .

But again and again and again when I travel around the country or read reader comments, I see educators languishing for lack of clear purpose. Every year in my classes, I see students of every background and ability level frustrated by what they see as the purposelessness of high school.

When I became a teacher in 2006, my purpose was vague: I wanted to “make a positive impact on students' lives.” Several years ago, I modified that into the clearer “Mount Everest” of promoting long-term student flourishing [1]. My working life is dedicated to that single purpose: every lesson I teach and word I write and workshop I lead is aimed at promoting long-term flourishing, either for my students or for yours.

Working from this clarity of purpose, I'm less likely to, as McKeown says, “waste time and energy on the trivial many.” Put positively, clarity of purpose makes me far more likely to do the right work, the work that benefits my students and my career long term.

Instead of “it's smart for me to be up each night until the wee hours grading essays,” I can prioritize things like sleep and family . After all, modeling how one lives a flourishing (and therefore balanced) life is one way I seek to promote long-term flourishing in my students.

But I can tell you, off the top of my head, what my purpose is, and I can give you examples of how I work toward that purpose day in and day out. Ask me one hundred times, “Dave, what are you ultimately driving at?” and I'll give you the same answer each time.
